Title: Verification checks specified requirements; validation checks the intended use
Caption: Conceptual systems-engineering trace. Verification compares objective evidence with specified requirements; validation evaluates the resulting system against stakeholder needs in its intended context. A10 Hz rate is an assigned example, not a validated device result. Requirements should identify units, conditions, tolerances, and an observable criterion.

Title: Functional analysis separates required behavior from interface implementation
Caption: Conceptual functional chain and two assigned interface examples. Required functions do not uniquely prescribe hardware. Interfaces need timing, units, range, direction, failure behavior, and ownership. Local component tests can miss interaction failures, so integration evidence belongs to the system boundary.

Title: Change control keeps the approved baseline traceable through an evaluated revision
Caption: Conceptual engineering change workflow. Authorization here is a system-design process step, not a request for user permission in this figure task. Rejected or deferred changes do not become the baseline. Configuration identification, controlled documents, status accounting, and verification preserve the relation between requirements, design, and tested product.

Title: FMEA identifies effects and actions; an RPN is only one prioritization aid
Caption: Assigned illustrative1–10 rating convention. RPN values96,90,60 are products of ordinal scores, not calibrated failure probabilities or expected monetary losses. Equal RPNs can conceal different severity and detection. Actions need an owner and verified effect; no rating reduction or risk acceptance is claimed before evidence.

Title: A fault tree distinguishes either-cause failure from simultaneous redundant-path failure
Caption: Logical OR and AND junctions are explicitly labeled. Mission failure probabilities are assigned and all three basic events are independent. OR requires subtracting the overlap; AND of pump failures gives.002. Shared causes, repair dynamics, or dependent events need a different calculation. The tree is simplified and does not demonstrate real-system reliability or protective performance.

Title: Independent series paths require every element; parallel paths require at least one
Caption: Assigned mission reliabilities at the same time and conditions. Independence and ideal success logic are required. Parallel success assumes either full- capacity path can deliver the function without switching failures or common causes. These reliability values are not steady-state availability and do not incorporate repairs during a mission.

Title: Availability includes repair; mission reliability and lifecycle risk answer other questions
Caption: Assigned alternating up/repair process with long-run mean up time1000 h and repair time10 h. The exponential mission curve additionally assumes a constant failure rate; the availability ratio alone does not require exponential distributions. Maintainability concerns restoration time, while lifecycle risk also combines consequence, environment, aging, and uncertainty. No safety conclusion follows from high availability.

Title: Rigid-body velocity combines translation of a reference point and rotation about it
Caption: Assigned planar instantaneous motion. The link position difference is(2,1) m; positive angular velocity is counterclockwise out of the page. Velocity arrows use explanatory drawing scales rather than a common velocity-diagram scale. Translation of A need not be perpendicular to AB; only the relative rotational velocity is perpendicular.

Title: The coupler instantaneous center lies where the two velocity-normal lines intersect
Caption: Same four-bar geometry as1266, at crank angle60°. Extending the crank and rocker directions locates the coupler/ground instantaneous center. It can lie outside the physical link and moves as the configuration changes. A point at the center has zero velocity only at that instant; its acceleration need not vanish. Speed-ratio statement applies to the coupler’s instantaneous rotation.

Title: Four-bar closure connects link lengths, configuration angles, and a coupler point
Caption: Assigned planar crank-rocker geometry with ground adjacent to the shortest link and an upper assembly branch. Link lengths and computed coordinates close exactly. Coupler point P is midpoint plus0.4 m normal offset. Grashof length inequality permits crank rotation for this topology; branch changes, transmission angle, collisions, and practical clearances need separate consideration.

Title: A slider-crank converts rotation into reciprocating displacement with stroke2r
Caption: Assigned in-line slider-crank, right-hand slider branch, r1 m and l3 m. Positive displacement is rightward from the crank pivot; positive crank angle is counterclockwise. vB is the time derivative of the exact slider position with ω2 rad/s. Guide lines denote the slider constraint, not friction or load capacity. Stroke is max x−min x=2r.

Title: External spur gears rotate in opposite directions while pitch-line speeds match
Caption: Ideal external spur-gear pair with common module, no slip at the pitch point, and parallel shafts. Dashed circles are pitch circles; actual tooth profiles are intentionally omitted. Angular velocities are signed about a common out-of-page axis. Tooth count, radius ratio, and speed ratio agree; torque requires efficiency and load assumptions not supplied here.

Title: Compound gearing multiplies stage ratios; planetary gearing uses speeds relative to the carrier
Caption: ωout/ωin=(20/40)(15/45)=+1/6

Title: Swept geometry and a toggle singularity impose distinct mechanism constraints
Caption: Left shades the convex hull of sampled centerline configurations, not a certified swept envelope: link thickness, intermediate positions, tolerances, and tooling need added clearance. Right is a separate ideal collinear two-link toggle, μ0° or180°, where a kinematic constraint becomes singular. The original four-bar is not claimed to reach that toggle. Numerical conditioning and branch choice need attention near singularities.

Title: An undamped mass-spring system oscillates at its natural frequency
Caption: Assigned linear, single-degree-of-freedom oscillator around static equilibrium with no damping or forcing. The damper symbol is retained but its coefficient is explicitly zero. Spring stiffness is200 N/m, mass2 kg, natural period2π/10 s. Displacement uses millimeters while equations for force require conversion to meters.

Title: Damping changes free-response shape while the initial displacement and velocity stay fixed
Caption: Assigned linear viscous damping and identical initial conditions for all curves. Underdamped motion uses ωd=ωn√(1−ζ²). Critical response is nonoscillatory; the chosen overdamped response returns more slowly. Shapes depend on initial conditions, so absence of overshoot alone does not identify the damping regime of an arbitrary record.

Title: Successive same-sign peaks provide logarithmic decrement for an underdamped decay
Caption: Synthetic decay record illustrates how measured peak amplitudes would be used; it is not experimental data. Same-sign peaks are one damped period apart, linear viscous damping and one dominant mode are assumed. The assigned model hasωn10 rad/s andζ.05. Noise, multiple modes, nonlinearity, or peak selection errors can invalidate the single-pair estimate.

Title: Harmonic force produces a steady displacement magnified relative to static deflection
Caption: Linear viscous-damped SDOF model with harmonic applied force. Curves are steady-state amplitudes after the transient decays; F0/k is static deflection. Resonant amplification depends on damping. Zero-damping resonance has no bounded steady-state amplitude and is not included. Phase lag, initial response, and nonlinear limits are separate.

Title: The displacement peak occurs below r=1 when damping is positive and sufficiently small
Caption: Same forced-displacement magnification convention as1274. The positive-frequency peak condition differs from merely settingω=ωn. Forζ≥1/√2 the maximum over r≥0 is at r0, M1. Curves are ideal linear-response functions, not machine operating limits or measured modal data.

Title: Force isolation begins above r=√2 for the ideal spring-damper mount
Caption: Assigned force-excited machine on linear mounts; transmitted force is the spring-plus-damper reaction amplitude at the base. Increased damping suppresses resonance but can increase high-frequency force transmission. The shaded region is mathematical isolation, not guaranteed performance of an actual multi- mode machine. Base-motion transmissibility uses a related expression but a different input/output definition.

Title: A Campbell diagram locates excitation-order crossings with natural-frequency bands
Caption: Assigned speed-independent frequency bands and excitation orders1,2,3. Dots mark crossings of order lines with nominal30 and60 Hz modes. Band intersections define speed intervals rather than single prohibited speeds. Actual resonant amplitude depends on forcing, damping, mode participation, and speed-dependent dynamics; a real rotor may have changing natural frequencies.

Title: A shoulder concentrates elastic stress above the nominal section stress
Caption: Axisymmetric shaft shown in axial section under tension. Lines illustrate redistribution rather than a solved stress field. Kt2 is assigned, not calculated from this drawn fillet geometry. Nominal area is the smaller section. Elastic concentration Kt differs from fatigue notch factor Kf; plasticity, size, surface finish, and loading affect practical assessment.

Title: Tresca and von Mises give different biaxial yield envelopes for the same yield strength
Caption: Ideal isotropic ductile yield criteria under plane stress with two nonzero principal stresses. Axes use the same scale and strength Sy. Interior points remain below the displayed yield criterion; no factor of safety, fatigue, instability, or fracture criterion is included. Tresca is the inner hexagon and the envelopes meet at uniaxial and equal-biaxial states.

Title: A Coulomb-Mohr brittle envelope distinguishes tensile and compressive strengths
Caption: Assigned brittle Coulomb-Mohr plane-stress model with third principal stress zero. In like-sign quadrants the extreme tensile/compressive principal stress controls; mixed-sign quadrants use the linear interaction shown. This is not the modified-Mohr criterion or a material-specific validated failure locus. The marked point is below this criterion only, without other failure checks or safety factors.

Title: A fluctuating stress cycle separates mean, amplitude, and stress ratio
Caption: Assigned sinusoidal cycle at2 Hz, tension positive. Mean50 and amplitude100 MPa yield150 maximum and−50 minimum. This is not fully reversed loading, which would have mean zero and R−1. Fatigue-life assessment also needs material, surface, geometry, loading history, and a mean-stress treatment; this plot defines cycle quantities only.

Title: Illustrative S–N trends distinguish an endurance region from continued strength decline
Caption: Synthetic curves illustrate shape, not test data or allowable stresses for a particular alloy. Logarithmic axes, constant-amplitude fully reversed loading, and assigned room-condition trends. Some steels show an endurance region under specified conditions; not every steel or environment does. Aluminum fatigue strength is commonly specified at a finite life. Scatter, mean stress, and environmental corrections are omitted.

Title: Mode-I stress intensity scales with tensile stress and the square root of crack size
Caption: Wide plate with a central through crack perpendicular to the applied tension, so a is half the total crack length. Assigned geometry factor1 represents an ideal wide-plate limit; the drawing is schematic. Linear-elastic, small-scale yielding and appropriate plane-strain toughness conditions are needed for KI/KIC assessment. The example does not exclude net-section yield, fatigue growth, or other failure modes.

Title: Creep progresses from a falling strain rate through a near-steady stage to accelerating strain
Caption: Assigned smooth qualitative creep-strain curve under nominally constant load and temperature; horizontal scale is normalized rather than hours. Stage boundaries are illustrative and depend on material and conditions. Initial elastic strain and an experimentally measured rupture time are not included. Increasing tertiary rate can involve damage and changing stress as the section deforms.

Title: A sand-casting mold provides a connected feed path and a riser for solidification shrinkage
Caption: Original simplified mold section, not a designed gating system. The sprue, runner, gate, cavity, and riser are connected; a hot spot is a candidate shrinkage location rather than a prediction. Porosity, inclusions, cold shuts, and shrinkage have different causes. Actual feeding, venting, alloy behavior, cooling modulus, and process parameters need evaluated geometry and evidence.

Title: Turning removes a radial depth while the workpiece rotates and the tool feeds axially
Caption: Assigned longitudinal external turning, tool advances left into the uncut20 mm diameter and leaves16 mm diameter behind it. Radial depth=(20−16)/2=2 mm. Cutting speed is specified at the initial diameter; it decreases at fixed rpm as diameter falls. Chip and tool geometry are schematic; machining feasibility also depends on material, tool, power, rigidity, and actual cutting conditions.

Title: Taylor tool life becomes a straight line on logarithmic speed-time axes
Caption: Assigned Taylor relation at fixed feed, depth, tool, material, and failure criterion. With T in minutes and V in m/min, C has compatible dimensional units and is numerically200; n is dimensionless. Plot axes are T horizontal and V vertical, giving slope−n. Reversing axes gives−1/n. Constants do not transfer automatically to another process or material.

Title: Metal forming changes cross-section by rolling, forging, pushing, or pulling
Caption: Four original forming schematics with exaggerated section changes. Rolling speeds follow constant-width incompressible volume flow; forging dashed outline denotes the earlier shape. Extrusion pushes a confined billet through a die; drawing pulls wire through a converging die. Tool motion, contact friction, and forming-load magnitudes are not solved.

Title: An equilibrium phase diagram and a heat-treatment time path answer different questions
Caption: Both diagrams are assigned teaching models, not an actual binary-alloy phase diagram or alloy-specific heat-treatment schedule. Liquidus/solidus meet at pure-component endpoints and bound an L+α field. The thermal path demonstrates heating, holding, rapid cooling, and reheating. Actual transformations require the alloy’s thermodynamics and time-temperature kinetics; no martensite or heat-treatment suitability is implied for this illustrative isomorphous system.
